newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU, U.S. fail to clinch deal in trade talks.
newsitem.headline: EU, U.S. fail to clinch deal in trade talks.

text.p: European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan failed to clinch a deal with the United States on Tuesday to simplify trade in pharmaceutical, medical, telecoms and other products.

Brittan, who had been hoping to overcome U.S. reticence in talks on the sidelines of an OECD summit here, put new proposals to U.S. Trade Secretary Charlene Barshefsky but did not manage to secure agreement despite what was described as a "narrowing of differences."

He was seeking to wrap up talks, which came to an impasse in Washington last week, so that pharmaceutical, medical, telecoms, electrical products and leisure craft certified as safe in the European Union would not need double-checking before entering the United States and vice-versa -- under so-called mutual recognition agreements (MRAs).

"We have made substantial progress on MRAs but it remains unclear whether the two sides can resolve all issues necessary to reach agreement at this juncture," Bershefsky said in a statement after their talks.
U.S. estimates put the overall value of trade in products that would be covered by such an agreement at $40 billion, according to an EU official.

Brittan did not divulge details of his new proposals but EU officials said they had yet to bridge the gap on pharmaceutical and medical devices, while agreement on telecommunications and electrical equipment has been largely worked out.
"We have made a lot of progress, but there are one or two points outstanding," an EU official told reporters.

Much of the disagreement centred on the U.S. Food and Drugs Administration (FDA), which is reluctant to give up its powers to accept or reject European products, although the FDA had been shifting its position during the talks, EU officials said.

U.S. officials said last week, when the talks stalled in Washington, that the FDA was concerned U.S. consumer safety would be threatened if the U.S. lost the right to have the final say on European products.
Earlier, EU officials said that they had set themselves the deadline of agreement by the time U.S. President Bill Clinton met European Comission President Jacques Santer on Wednesday.
Brittan, who represents the European Union in several international trade talk forums, said the EU had recently struck an MRA deal with Canada.
